newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian premiers to meet on rival troop clashes.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian premiers to meet on rival troop clashes.

text.p: Cambodian First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Thursday said he would meet co-Premier Hun Sen to try to halt clashes between coalition forces which he said had killed soldiers on both sides.

Ranariddh told reporters on his return from Europe that he would discuss the volatile political situation in the northwest province of Battambang with Second Prime Minister Hun Sen at a scheduled meeting of the cabinet on Friday.
The two parties formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.

The prince said there had been casualties in this week's clashes between members of his royalist FUNCINPEC party and soldiers of Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP), the former communist government.

His deputy commander in the region, General Thlang Sovanarith, said that since Tuesday, 16 CPP soldiers had been killed and 19 wounded. Three FUNCINPEC soldiers were killed, including a deputy commander of military operations.

"I like to play (the situation) down because the most important thing is the development of the country," said Ranariddh, speaking a day after Hun Sen had also tried to make light of the latest clashes in the rice-bowl province.
CPP co-Minister of Defence Tea Banh dimissed the clashes as minor land disputes and said there had been no casualties.
"We (CPP) have not provoked any problems with others," he told Reuters.
A military analyst said the two sides were testing their relative strength and predicted more such incidents ahead of local and general elections due in 1997 and 1998.

Relations between CPP and FUNCINPEC plummeted in November after clashes between the two sides in Battambang left several wounded and ill feelings have continued to simmer despite the intervention of senior officials from both sides.

Their armies were merged in 1993 when Ranariddh and Hun Sen agreed to share power, but analysts say their forces maintain their pre-coalition loyalties and continue to reflect the rivalries between the two leaders.
